sentences: A commander on a white horse leads his cavalry forward into battle.
On the ground, broken lances lie in a strangely tidy pattern.
This is The Battle of San Romano, by the Florentine painter Paolo Uccello.
It was probably painted around 1438 to 1440, in egg tempera with some oil on panels of poplar wood.
It is a huge picture, 182 centimetres high and 320 centimetres wide, and the National Gallery in London bought it in 1857.
Look first at the rider on the white horse in the centre.
He is Niccolò da Tolentino, commander of the Florentine army.
He wears a magnificent red and gold hat and thrusts his baton forward.
He is one of the very few figures whose face is uncovered, while the others keep their visors down.
The picture celebrates the Battle of San Romano in the summer of 1432, when Florence defeated forces fighting on the side of Siena.
At the far left, a row of mounted trumpeters sounds the charge, while on the right a knight on a white horse fights off three opponents at once.
Now look at the ground.
The broken lances lie like a grid, running in lines towards a single invisible vanishing point.
Even a dead soldier, lying face down, is stretched out along these lines.
This is Uccello experimenting with linear perspective, which was still a recent discovery in his day.
Look also at the hedge behind the soldiers, dotted with pink and white roses, oranges and pomegranates.
The painting has darkened a great deal over time, but it once sparkled with silver leaf and brilliant colours.
This was originally one of three panels, made for the palace of the wealthy Salimbeni family, who had moved to Florence from Siena.
Later, Lorenzo de' Medici took the panels by force, had their arched tops cut down to rectangles, and hung them in his own palace.
The inventory drawn up in 1492, the year Lorenzo died, records the three panels hanging together in his room.
Today they are scattered: one is in the National Gallery in London, one in the Uffizi in Florence, and one in the Louvre in Paris.

This winter, however, from 3 December 2026 to 1 March 2027, an exhibition at the Pitti Palace in Florence brings the three panels together for the first time in history, so visitors can see them as they once hung in the Medici palace.
Uccello was born around 1397 and died in 1475.
Step back and look again.
Instead of blood and chaos, we see knights arranged like decoration and a grid laid across the ground.
Think about how, when we remember a chaotic moment, we too redraw it with some kind of order.
